intent: Show the single architectural change: a transformer attention layer that emits four projections (Q, K, V, Forecast) instead of three, with the Forecast feeding the NEXT layer's block selector.
description: Side-by-side comparison of two transformer attention layers, drawn as clean block diagrams. LEFT panel titled 'Standard sparse attention layer': input arrow labeled 'X_l (hidden state)' enters a box labeled 'Linear projection' which emits three labeled arrows: Q, K, V. The Q arrow splits into TWO paths: one into a box 'Top-k block selector' and one into a box 'Sparse attention'; the selector box outputs 'selected KV blocks' into the sparse attention box; then an arrow to 'FFN' and out. A dashed rounded rectangle encloses everything, labeled 'layer l — selection and attention both wait for Q'. Small warning annotation under the left panel: 'Q only exists once the layer is already running → too late to fetch anything early'. RIGHT panel titled 'SparDA layer': same layout but the Linear projection box emits FOUR labeled arrows: Q, K, V, and F (Forecast), with F drawn in a distinct accent color. Q goes ONLY into 'Sparse attention'. The F arrow curves forward and EXITS the dashed layer boundary toward the right, labeled 'F_l → selects blocks for layer l+1'. A matching accent arrow enters this layer's 'Top-k block selector' from the left, labeled 'F_(l-1) from previous layer'. Bottom takeaway banner spanning both panels: 'One extra projection decouples WHAT TO FETCH from DOING THE ATTENTION — selection moves one layer ahead.'

intent: Explain the two problems of sparse attention with an offloaded KV cache: the PCIe copy stall at every layer, and the growing cost of block selection itself.
description: Two-panel diagram of the two problems that SparDA fixes. PANEL A titled 'Problem 1 — the PCIe stall': two columns, 'GPU memory (small, fast)' on the left and 'CPU RAM (big, slow)' on the right. In CPU RAM draw a tall stack of many small rectangles labeled 'KV cache — grows with every generated token (100K+ context)'. A thick arrow labeled 'copy selected KV blocks over PCIe' crosses from CPU RAM to GPU. Below the columns, a horizontal timeline of one decode step: alternating segments 'layer 1 compute' (dark), 'wait for copy' (red hatched), 'layer 2 compute' (dark), 'wait for copy' (red hatched), 'layer 3 compute' with the red segments labeled 'GPU sits idle — stall repeats at EVERY layer of EVERY token'. PANEL B titled 'Problem 2 — the selection tax': a single query token (small circle labeled 'q, one token per decode step') pointing at a long row of candidate blocks labeled 'scored KV blocks (thousands at long context)'. Multiple parallel arrows fan out from a bracket labeled 'every query head in the GQA group scores every block', followed by small boxes 'softmax per head' then 'sum across heads' then 'top-k'. Caption inside panel: 'the attention itself is cheap during decode — DECIDING what to attend to is what grows with context length'. Bottom takeaway banner: 'Both problems trace to one design choice: the attention query Q drives block selection.'

intent: Show the payoff of one-layer-ahead selection: the CPU-to-GPU copy overlaps with the current layer's compute on a separate CUDA stream, so the GPU never waits.
description: Timeline diagram comparing decode execution without and with lookahead prefetch, drawn as horizontal swimlanes with time flowing left to right. TOP half titled 'Query-driven selection (no lookahead)': ONE single lane where blocks strictly alternate: 'select blocks for layer 2' (small), 'COPY layer-2 KV from CPU' (red hatched, wide, labeled 'GPU idle'), 'compute layer 2' (dark), then again 'select for layer 3', 'COPY layer-3 KV' (red hatched, 'GPU idle'), 'compute layer 3'. Annotation: 'copy and compute serialize — total time = compute + copy'. BOTTOM half titled 'SparDA (one-layer-ahead Forecast)': TWO parallel lanes. Lane 1 labeled 'compute stream (GPU)': continuous back-to-back dark blocks 'compute layer 1', 'compute layer 2', 'compute layer 3', 'compute layer 4' with NO gaps. Lane 2 labeled 'prefetch stream (PCIe copy)': accent-colored blocks 'copy blocks for layer 2', 'copy blocks for layer 3', 'copy blocks for layer 4', each positioned directly UNDER the previous layer's compute block, showing overlap. Curved arrows from each compute block down to the next copy block, labeled 'Forecast F_l announces layer l+1 blocks early'. Annotation: 'copy hides behind compute — total time ≈ compute only'. Bottom takeaway banner: 'The persistent UVA kernel streams KV blocks in parallel with the math: latency of offloading, hidden.'

intent: Show the second win: because the Forecast is not the attention query, selection needs only ONE head per GQA group and can skip softmax entirely, cutting selection cost up to 2.5x.
description: Side-by-side comparison of block-selection machinery. LEFT panel titled 'Baseline selector — query does the choosing': a GQA group drawn as 8 small stacked squares labeled 'G = 8 query heads (share one KV head)'; from EACH of the 8 heads an arrow goes to a wide row of candidate blocks labeled 'compressed KV blocks', creating a dense fan of 8 scoring passes; then a box 'softmax (per head)', then a box 'sum scores across 8 heads', then 'max-pool to block level', then 'top-k'. Cost tag in a corner: '8 scoring passes + softmax + reduction — every decode step'. RIGHT panel titled 'SparDA Forecast indexer — one skinny head': a SINGLE accent-colored square labeled '1 Forecast head per GQA group (one per KV head)' with a single clean arrow to the same row of candidate blocks, then straight to 'top-k'. Two small crossed-out boxes beside it: 'softmax — skipped' and 'per-head loop — gone'. Stat callouts on the right panel: 'block-selection cost: up to 2.50x lower at 128K' and 'decode-time selection stays nearly FLAT as context grows'. Bottom takeaway banner: 'Selection stops paying rent for the attention query's multi-head layout.'

intent: Explain how the Forecast is trained: the 8B backbone stays frozen, only 33.5M Forecast parameters learn, by KL-matching the original selector's block-attention distribution.
description: Training diagram for the Forecast projections, drawn as a distillation setup. CENTER: a large grey rounded rectangle labeled 'sparse-pretrained 8B backbone — FROZEN (99.6% of weights)' with a small snowflake icon; attached along its side, several small accent-colored tabs labeled 'Forecast projections — TRAINED, 33.5M params (0.41%)'. LEFT branch titled 'Teacher (the original selector)': arrow from the backbone to a small bar chart of block probabilities labeled 'block-attention distribution from the real query heads (fine-grained targets: kernel 2, stride 1)'. RIGHT branch titled 'Student (the Forecast)': arrow from the accent tabs to a second bar chart labeled 'Forecast scores for the SAME blocks, predicted one layer ahead'. Between the two bar charts, a double-headed arrow labeled 'KL divergence loss — over the top-k blocks + one REST bucket for everything else'. Footer strip with three fact chips: '2,000 training steps', 'ProLong-64K long-context data', 'no backbone retraining — plugs into existing models'. Bottom takeaway banner: 'The Forecast learns to imitate tomorrow's selector, today.'

intent: Present the headline results as a scoreboard: accuracy holds or improves, decode gets 1.7x faster, and freed GPU memory buys 5.3x throughput via bigger batches.
description: Results scoreboard drawn as three large card panels with the numbers written in as big display figures (no plotted axes, just labeled cards and mini bar comparisons). CARD 1 titled 'Accuracy — nothing lost': lines reading 'MiniCPM4.1-8B: +0.3 avg over sparse baseline', 'NOSA-8B: +2.3 avg', a highlighted chip '+6.5 on long reasoning (NOSA-8B)', and 'RULER gap over baseline WIDENS with length: +1.7 at 32K → +4.3 at 128K'. CARD 2 titled 'Latency — vs sparse offload baseline (H100, 128K context)': two thick horizontal comparison bars: 'prefill: 1.25x faster' and 'decode: up to 1.7x faster', with a small footnote 'selection cheaper + copy hidden behind compute'. CARD 3 titled 'Throughput — the memory dividend': mini diagram showing a GPU box where 'KV cache moved to CPU RAM' frees space filled by many stacked request rows labeled 'batch 64 fits (non-offload sparse OOMs at batch 4-8)'; big numbers '5.3x decode throughput vs non-offload sparse' and '9.2x vs dense'. Bottom takeaway banner: 'Same accuracy, 1.7x faster decode, and the freed GPU memory becomes batch size.'
